lesson.title: The Leftover That Tells You How Good the Line Really Is
lesson.summary: A residual is the gap between what actually happened and what the regression line predicted, and looking at every residual together is how you judge whether a line truly fits.
lesson.body:
A residual is the leftover difference between what actually happened and what the regression line predicted for that same individual, computed as residual equals actual y minus predicted y, or e equals y minus y-hat. Every point in the original data set has its own residual, since every point has both a real observed value that was measured and a value the line would have predicted for that same x, whether the line fits well there or not.

The sign of a residual carries direct meaning right on the scatterplot. A positive residual means the actual point sits above the regression line, so the model underpredicted that individual's real value. A negative residual means the actual point sits below the line, so the model overpredicted. Geometrically, a residual is exactly the vertical distance from a data point up or down to the line, which connects directly back to how the regression line itself was defined in an earlier chapter, as the one line minimizing the sum of those squared vertical distances across every point.

Computing residuals for all five students using predicted score equals 39 plus 10 times hours studied: at 1 hour, predicted is 49, actual is 50, residual is 1. At 2 hours, predicted is 59, actual is 60, residual is 1. At 3 hours, predicted is 69, actual is 65, residual is negative 4. At 4 hours, predicted is 79, actual is 80, residual is 1. At 5 hours, predicted is 89, actual is 90, residual is 1. Adding all five residuals together, 1 plus 1 minus 4 plus 1 plus 1, gives exactly 0.

That sum of zero is not a coincidence specific to this one data set, it is a guaranteed property of every least squares line ever fit, a direct mathematical consequence of how b0 and b1 were originally chosen to minimize the sum of squared residuals. It is the same underlying fact, seen from a different angle, that guarantees the regression line always passes through the point formed by the mean of x and the mean of y, discussed in an earlier chapter.

Beyond simply checking that the residuals sum to zero, plotting every residual against its corresponding x-value produces a residual plot, one of the most useful diagnostic tools in all of regression analysis. If the residuals scatter randomly above and below zero with no visible pattern left over, the straight line model is a reasonable description of the data. If instead the residuals trace out a clear curve, for example strongly positive at both low and high x-values and negative in the middle, that leftover pattern is a warning sign that the true relationship was never actually linear to begin with, the exact kind of structure the earlier U-shaped, squared distance example would produce unmistakably in its own residuals.

This is also why the method from several chapters back is named least squares regression in the first place. The fitted line was chosen specifically to make the sum of the squared version of these same residual values as small as it could possibly be, out of every line that could have been drawn, tying the name of the method directly back to the exact quantity examined in this chapter.
